I just opened PR #4377 to add Stephen Wolfram's Rule 30 problems.

The first two are quite easy, but I'm wondering if anyone here has an idea on how to formalize problem 3:

Does computing the nth cell of the center column require at least O(n) computational effort?

Wolfram gives formal description of the problem in Mathematica but I am a bit stumped on what is the best way to translate it into lean.
@Justus Springer didn't you formalise the statement of an Annals paper which was of this nature?
"at least O(n)" is nonsense. Surely Wolfram means "Omega(n)".

Here is the Mathematica code he provides:

¬∃ m, ( ∀ n, machine[m][n]〚1〛== last[c[n]] ) ∧ limsup [machine[m][n]〚2〛/ n, n->∞] )

where

  • m is a turing machine
  • machine[m][n]〚1〛== last[c[n]] is the nth entry in the sequence
  • machine[m][n]〚2〛 is the "amount of computational effort taken (e.g. number of steps)"
    He also specifies that

one should also require that m be finite, so the machine’s rule can’t just store the answer

Does a finite m actually preclude "rule can't just store the answer" , except in the most trivial sense? Or is that a well defined 'iff'?

It seems like a pretty broad context( more than vanilla Turing machine, considering "imagine that we have a particular Turing machine (or some other computational system)" ?).

Should the hypothesis not actually just be encoding exactly "rule can't just store the answer", rather than specifying that restrictive case ( a lot more infinities than finities)? I am no expert though.
